idea: When to replace old plumbing pipes
title: Identifying Internal Pipe Tuberculation
description: Educational tip demonstrating why galvanized steel supply pipes require replacement due to internal tuberculation and severe mineral scale accumulation.
image_prompt: A professional macro photograph in vertical 9:16 aspect ratio showing a cleanly cut section of an old 3/4-inch galvanized steel water pipe held by a plumber wearing clean work gloves. The cross-section directly reveals severe internal tuberculation, showing thick layers of orange, brown, and dark red rust corrosion and mineral scaling that almost completely block the inner pipe channel, leaving only a tiny central hole for water flow. The outer metallic surface of the pipe appears relatively intact, highlighting the contrast between outer appearance and internal blockages. Clean daylight lighting, sharp focus on the internal lumen structure, neutral workshop background with shallow depth of field. No text, no logos, no watermarks, no artificial diagrams.
visual_story: The viewer immediately notices a cross-section of an old galvanized steel water pipe. While the exterior metal wall looks solid and intact, the interior lumen is nearly completely choked with rust deposits and mineral buildup (tuberculation). This visual demonstrates why evaluating pipe health purely from the outside can be misleading, as internal restriction drastically reduces water volume and pressure throughout the supply system.

on_image_text.hook: Old Pipes Can Look Fine Outside But Be Choked Inside
on_image_text.explanation: Galvanized steel pipes corrode internally over time, forming thick rust layers that restrict water flow and drop water pressure.
on_image_text.takeaway: Persistent low water volume across multiple fixtures often indicates severe internal pipe corrosion requiring piping replacement.
